newsitem.title: UK: EU's Brittan warns over Euro-sceptic UK election.
newsitem.headline: EU's Brittan warns over Euro-sceptic UK election.

text.p: European Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan warned Britain's politicians on Friday that whipping up anti-European sentiment in the coming election campaign could hamstring Britain in crucial negotiations over Europe's future.

Speaking during a visit to London, Brittan also cautioned that the idea of flexibility arrangements to let some European Union members forge ahead on their own in certain areas could result in Britain becoming dangerously isolated.
"Don't damage Britain by engaging in a Dutch auction of Euro-scepticism," Brittan, a former Conservative cabinet minister, told a small group of reporters.

Doing so would make it immeasurably harder for Britain to get its way at June's EU summit in Amsterdam, when the long-running inter-governmental conference on how to reform the bloc's institutions is due to conclude.

Brittan said he had conveyed his warning, in face-to-face meetings and in public speeches, both to Prime Minister John Major's ruling Conservatives and to the main opposition Labour party led by Tony Blair.

Major has said he will make Europe one of the three central planks of his election campaign -- along with constitutional change and the economy -- in an attempt to highlight policy differences with Labour, which enjoys a commanding poll lead.
But Brittan said that trying to establish clear blue water over Europe simply would not work for Major.

With the exception of its vow to sign the European social chapter on workers' rights, Labour would simply "creep up" on the Conservatives if Major adopted a more Euro-sceptical stance, Brittan predicted.

Despite his fears of a drift to a more hostile attitude to Brussels, Brittan said he did not expect Major to close off the option of joining a single European currency on its scheduled starting date of January 1, 1999.
"I don't believe there will be any change in the present (wait-and-see) formula, and I think it would be unwise to make such a change," Brittan said.

He briskly dismissed as "out of the ballpark" a front-page report this week in Britain's Independent newspaper that said France and Germany were spearheading plans to harmonise the EU's tax and social security regimes.

Brittan acknowledged that the concept of flexibility as a way of reconciling different visions of how the EU should develop was unwelcome to the Brussels-based European Commission, the 15-member EU's executive arm.

Although the momentum that had built up behind the idea meant it could not now be ignored, he said granting a majority of states the flexibility to forge ahead without others should be very much the exception rather than the rule.

Brittan said it should be possible to find a formula to reconcile the different views of flexibility represented by a wary Britain on the one hand and keen integrationists France and Germany on the other hand.
But in another warning to Major, who said this week he was confident of breaking the deadlock, Brittan said: "It is not a panacea to our problems. It can be a trap and a risk."

If Britain opted out time after time of new policy initiatives, the end result could be the very nightmare its foreign policy has tried to head off for the past 300 years -- the creation of a continental block over which it has no sway.
